concepts.title: Scene safety
key_points: Scene safety begins before you arrive and never stops while you are there
The order is you, your crew, the patient, then bystanders — in that order, every time
An injured EMT stops being a rescuer and becomes a second patient
If the scene is not safe and you cannot make it safe, you stage and wait for the resource that can
Scenes change: a quiet scene can turn while you are kneeling on it
misconceptions: Entering a scene because the patient looks critical
Treating scene safety as a box ticked on arrival rather than a continuous process
Assuming law enforcement being present means the scene is secure

read.plain:
Scene safety is the first thing and it is not a step you finish. It starts with the dispatch information, continues as you pull up and look at the address, and carries on the entire time you are there.

The order matters and it is always the same: you, then your crew, then your patient, then everyone else standing around. That ordering feels wrong to people who came into this work to help, but an injured EMT does not help anybody. They become a second patient, they consume the resources that were coming for the first one, and now nobody is being treated.

If a scene is unsafe and you cannot make it safe with what you have, you do not go in. You stage a safe distance away and you wait for whoever can make it safe — law enforcement, the fire suppression crew, the power company. Waiting feels terrible. Do it anyway.

And keep looking. The dog that was asleep wakes up. The family member who was calm gets a phone call. The car that was stable shifts. Size-up is a loop, not a line.
read.standard: Scene safety is the initial and ongoing assessment of hazards to responders, patients and bystanders, and is the first component of the scene size-up. The established priority order is provider safety, crew safety, patient safety and bystander safety. An injured provider both removes a rescuer from the response and generates an additional patient, consuming resources allocated to the original incident. Where hazards exceed the crew's capability to mitigate them, the appropriate action is to stage at a safe distance and request the resource capable of securing the scene. Scene assessment is continuous rather than a discrete arrival step, as hazards may develop or be revealed during patient contact.

eli_new.analogy: Putting on your own oxygen mask first is not selfishness. It is the only way you are any use to anyone else.
eli_new.body: The instinct when someone is hurt is to run toward them. Every rule about scene safety exists to override that instinct, because the moment you are hurt too, the call stops being a rescue and becomes a bigger emergency with fewer people to handle it.

teach.prompt: Explain the order of priority in scene safety and why the order is what it is.

must_hit.point: You, then crew, then patient, then bystanders
An injured EMT becomes a second patient
Stage and wait if it cannot be made safe
Size-up is continuous

teach.model_answer: You first, then your crew, then the patient, then bystanders — in that order every time. It feels backwards for people who came into this work to help, but an injured EMT stops being a rescuer and becomes a second patient, consuming the very resources that were coming for the first one. If a scene is not safe and you cannot make it safe with what you have, you stage a safe distance away and wait for whoever can secure it. And it is not a box you tick on arrival: scenes change while you are kneeling on them, so you keep looking the whole time.

story.title: The dog in the back room
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — 60-year-old male, chest pain, private residence.
story.body:
The scene was fine. Calm house, calm family, patient sitting up talking to you.

Then somebody opened the back door to let the crew in with the stretcher and the dog came through it. Nobody had mentioned a dog. Nobody had asked.

Your partner got between it and you, the daughter grabbed the collar, and it was over in four seconds. But for those four seconds nobody was treating the chest pain.

concepts.title: Determining standard precautions
key_points: Standard precautions are chosen during size-up, before you touch the patient
Gloves are the baseline for every patient contact
Add eye protection whenever splashing or spraying is possible
Add a mask for a coughing or feverish patient, and consider one for the patient too
Add a gown when heavy contamination is likely, such as childbirth or major bleeding
The decision is made from the information you have, then upgraded as you learn more
misconceptions: Deciding on precautions after seeing how messy it is
Using gloves alone during suctioning or childbirth
Treating precautions as being about the patient's diagnosis rather than about the task
exam_favorites: That the decision is made before contact
Gown for childbirth and major bleeding

read.plain:
The decision about what to put on is part of the size-up, not a reaction to what you find. By the time you are close enough to know it is messy, you have already been exposed.

Gloves go on for every patient, always. Beyond that, you are matching the protection to the task rather than to the patient's diagnosis. Anything that could splash or spray toward your face — suctioning, active vomiting, arterial bleeding, childbirth — gets eye protection. A patient who is coughing or febrile gets a mask, and so do you. Heavy contamination, meaning a delivery or a major bleed, gets a gown.

The thing to hold onto is that you are protecting yourself from the job, not from a person. You almost never know what someone has. You do know whether you are about to put a suction catheter in their mouth.

And you upgrade as you go. If the call turns out to be more than dispatch described, stop and add what you need.
read.standard: Selection of standard precautions occurs during the scene size-up, prior to patient contact, and is based on the anticipated task rather than on presumed patient diagnosis. Gloves constitute the minimum for all patient contact. Eye protection is indicated where splash or spray is foreseeable, including suctioning, active vomiting, uncontrolled hemorrhage and childbirth. A surgical mask is indicated for patients with cough or fever, with source control by masking the patient where tolerated. Gown or fluid-resistant protection is indicated where gross contamination is anticipated. Precaution level is escalated as additional information emerges during the call.

eli_new.analogy: You dress for the job you are about to do, not for the person you are about to meet.
eli_new.body: You will almost never know what a patient is carrying. What you do know, before you get out of the truck, is roughly what you are going to be doing with your hands. That is what decides the gear.

teach.prompt: Explain how you decide what protective equipment to put on, and when you decide it.

must_hit.point: Decided during size-up, before patient contact
Gloves for every patient
Eye protection where splashing is possible
Mask for cough or fever; gown for heavy contamination

teach.model_answer: You decide during the size-up, before you touch anyone, because by the time you can see it is messy you have already been exposed. Gloves go on for every patient without exception. Then you match the rest to the task, not to the patient's diagnosis: eye protection anywhere splashing or spraying is possible — suctioning, vomiting, major bleeding, childbirth — a mask if they are coughing or febrile, and a mask on them too if they will tolerate it, and a gown where heavy contamination is likely. Then you upgrade as the call reveals itself.

story.title: Gloves only
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — female, abdominal pain, second floor.
story.body:
Dispatch said abdominal pain, so the crew went up with gloves.

She was 38 weeks pregnant and crowning.

The delivery went fine. What did not go fine was that two people spent the next hour in the decontamination room and one of them had to have a conversation with the infection control officer about eye protection.

concepts.title: Nature of illness versus mechanism of injury
key_points: Nature of illness is why a medical patient called; mechanism of injury is what physically happened to a trauma patient
The distinction steers the whole assessment: medical patients get a focused exam driven by the history, trauma patients get an exam driven by the mechanism
The information comes from the scene, the patient, family and bystanders
Some patients are both: a diabetic who crashed a car has a nature of illness and a mechanism
Never let the obvious injury hide the medical cause that produced it
misconceptions: Assuming a patient found in a car is purely a trauma patient
Deciding the nature of illness from dispatch information alone
Ignoring the scene because the patient can talk

read.plain:
Every patient falls broadly into two camps, and which camp they are in changes how you assess them.

A medical patient has a nature of illness — chest pain, difficulty breathing, altered mental status. You find it out mostly by asking, and the history drives a focused examination of whatever system is involved.

A trauma patient has a mechanism of injury — the physical forces that acted on them. You work it out mostly by looking: the height of the fall, the damage to the vehicle, the bent steering wheel, the starred windscreen. The mechanism drives what you examine, because it tells you where the energy went.

The interesting patients are the ones who are both. A driver who crashed into a parked car in the middle of the afternoon on an empty road has a mechanism of injury, yes. But ask why. Did they have a seizure? A stroke? Were they hypoglycemic? The crash is the consequence; something caused it.

That is the trap worth remembering. Blood and broken glass are loud. The quiet medical problem underneath them is what kills the patient later.
read.standard: The nature of illness (NOI) describes the medical complaint or condition prompting the call, while the mechanism of injury (MOI) describes the forces producing trauma. The distinction determines assessment strategy: the medical patient receives a history-driven focused examination, whereas the trauma patient receives an examination directed by the mechanism and its anticipated injury pattern. Information is derived from the scene, the patient, family and bystanders. Patients frequently present with both — a medical event precipitating a traumatic one — and the presence of obvious injury must not preclude investigation of an underlying medical cause, which may represent the more significant threat.

eli_new.analogy: The crash is the punchline. Always ask what the joke was.
eli_new.body: Injuries are visible and illnesses usually are not, so injuries get all the attention. The discipline is to look at an obviously injured patient and still ask why this happened today, to this person, in this place.

teach.prompt: Explain the difference between nature of illness and mechanism of injury, and why a patient can have both.

must_hit.point: NOI is the medical complaint; MOI is the physical forces
NOI drives a history-led exam; MOI drives an exam led by the forces
A medical event can cause a traumatic one

teach.model_answer: Nature of illness is why a medical patient called — chest pain, trouble breathing, altered mental status — and you find it by asking, with the history driving a focused exam of the system involved. Mechanism of injury is what physically happened to a trauma patient, and you find it by looking at the scene: the height of the fall, the damage to the car, the bent wheel. The mechanism tells you where the energy went and therefore where to examine. Plenty of patients are both — a driver who crashed because they had a seizure has a mechanism and a nature of illness — and the visible injury must never stop you asking what caused the crash.

story.title: Why today
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — single vehicle into a parked car, low speed, driver conscious.
story.body:
Minor damage. He is out of the car, walking, apologetic, saying he must have been distracted.

Your partner keeps asking why. Not what hurts — why. Empty road, dry, daylight, no phone in his hand.

His blood sugar comes back low enough that the crash makes sense. He was not distracted. He was going out.

rows.right: Exam led by where the energy went

concepts.title: Number of patients and additional resources
key_points: Count the patients before you commit to treating one
Ask for extra resources early; it is easy to cancel a unit and slow to summon one
The count includes people who have walked away, are still in a vehicle, or are not complaining
More patients than your crew can manage means you are running a multiple-casualty incident and triage applies
Resources are not only ambulances: law enforcement, fire suppression, power, rescue and air medical are all resources
misconceptions: Committing to the first patient you see and never counting
Waiting until you are overwhelmed before calling for help
Counting only the people who are complaining

read.plain:
Before you kneel down next to anybody, count. It is the step most easily skipped, because the first patient you see is usually the loudest one and your attention goes straight to them.

The count has to include people who are not obvious. Someone who climbed out and is sitting on the kerb. A child still in a rear-facing seat. A second occupant thrown clear. A family member who is quietly having a cardiac event from the stress. The quiet ones are routinely missed.

If the number of patients is more than your crew can handle, the call is no longer a patient-care call. It is a multiple-casualty incident, and you switch to triage.

When you ask for more, ask early. A unit you called and no longer need takes ten seconds to cancel. A unit you should have called ten minutes ago takes ten minutes to arrive, and those are ten minutes you spend without it.

And resources are broader than ambulances. Law enforcement for a scene that is not secure. Fire for a vehicle that is not stable. The power company for the wire nobody noticed. Rescue for entrapment. Air medical for distance or time.
read.standard: Determination of the number of patients occurs during the scene size-up and precedes commitment to individual patient care. The count must include patients who have self-extricated, remain within vehicles, or are not voicing complaint, as these are commonly overlooked. Where patient numbers exceed the capability of the responding crew, the incident is managed as a multiple-casualty incident and triage protocols apply. Requests for additional resources should be made early, as cancellation is trivial and delayed summoning is not. Resources encompass law enforcement, fire suppression, utility services, technical rescue and air medical assets in addition to further transporting units.

eli_new.analogy: It is quick to send a truck home. It is slow to get one to come.
eli_new.body: The first patient you see grabs your whole attention, which is exactly the problem. The step is to stand still for a few seconds, look around the whole scene, and count — including the people who are not asking for anything.

teach.prompt: Explain why you count patients before treating anyone, and what you do if there are more than you can manage.

must_hit.point: Count before committing to a patient
Include people who walked away or are not complaining
Call for resources early because cancelling is easy
More than you can manage means MCI and triage

teach.model_answer: You count first because the moment you kneel next to someone, your attention is gone. The count has to include the people who are not obvious — someone who climbed out and is sitting on the kerb, a child still in a car seat, a relative quietly having their own event. If there are more patients than your crew can manage, it stops being a patient-care call and becomes a multiple-casualty incident, and you switch to triage. Ask for extra resources early: cancelling a unit takes ten seconds, summoning one you needed ten minutes ago takes ten minutes. And resources means police, fire, power, rescue and air medical too, not just more ambulances.

story.title: The one on the kerb
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — two-vehicle collision, injuries reported.
story.body:
Two cars, one obviously worse. The driver of the worse one was screaming, so that is where everyone went.

Twenty minutes later somebody noticed the woman sitting quietly on the kerb forty feet away, who had been the front passenger in the other car and had walked there herself.

She had not said anything because she did not want to be a nuisance. Her spleen had other ideas.

concepts.title: Significant versus non-significant mechanism of injury
key_points: A significant mechanism is one where the forces involved make serious internal injury plausible, whether or not it is visible
A significant mechanism changes the assessment: rapid full-body scan rather than a focused exam

Commonly cited significant mechanisms include falls from height, ejection, death of another occupant, rollover, high-speed collision, penetrating trauma to the trunk, and being struck as a pedestrian or cyclist
Children and older adults sustain serious injury from lesser mechanisms than a healthy adult
Mechanism raises suspicion; it does not make a diagnosis, and a reassuring exam does not cancel a significant mechanism
misconceptions: Downgrading a significant mechanism because the patient looks fine
Applying adult mechanism thresholds to a child or an older adult
Treating mechanism as a diagnosis rather than as an index of suspicion
exam_favorites: That it drives rapid scan versus focused exam

read.plain:
The forces that acted on a patient tell you how much energy went into them, and energy is what injures. A significant mechanism of injury is one where the amount of energy makes serious internal injury plausible even if there is nothing to see.

The list you will be asked about is fairly consistent: a fall from a substantial height, ejection from a vehicle, another occupant in the same vehicle dying, a rollover, a high-speed collision, penetrating injury to the head, neck, chest or abdomen, and any pedestrian or cyclist struck by a vehicle. Confirm the exact thresholds your text uses, because the numbers attached to some of them vary.

What it changes is the shape of your assessment. Significant mechanism means you do a rapid scan of the whole body looking for injuries you have not been told about, rather than a focused examination of the part that hurts.

Two groups shift the threshold downward. Children get seriously hurt by forces that would leave an adult walking, and older adults are fragile in ways that a mechanism description does not capture. A fall from standing height is trivial for a twenty-year-old and can be lethal at eighty.

And the most important discipline: a significant mechanism is not cancelled by a patient who looks well. It raises your suspicion, and suspicion is not something the patient can talk you out of.
read.standard: Mechanism of injury is classified as significant where the forces involved make serious occult injury plausible irrespective of external findings. Commonly cited significant mechanisms include falls from height, ejection from a vehicle, death of another occupant in the same vehicle, vehicle rollover, high-velocity collision, penetrating trauma to the head, neck, torso or abdomen, and pedestrian or cyclist struck by a vehicle; specific thresholds vary between texts and trauma systems. Classification determines assessment strategy, with significant mechanism indicating a rapid full-body scan rather than a focused examination. Pediatric and geriatric patients sustain significant injury at lower energy thresholds, and age modifies the classification accordingly. Mechanism constitutes an index of suspicion rather than a diagnosis, and a reassuring initial examination does not negate a significant mechanism.

eli_new.analogy: Mechanism tells you how hard the bell was rung. It does not tell you whether the bell is cracked — but it tells you to go and look.
eli_new.body: New EMTs want the patient's appearance to settle the question, because a patient who is walking and talking feels like a patient who is fine. Mechanism exists precisely because internal injuries are quiet at first. The forces are evidence you can trust before the body has started showing you anything.

teach.prompt: Explain what makes a mechanism of injury significant, what it changes about your assessment, and why a patient who looks fine does not cancel it.

must_hit.point: Forces make serious internal injury plausible even with nothing visible
Examples: fall from height, ejection, rollover, death of an occupant, penetrating trunk injury, struck pedestrian
Drives a rapid full-body scan rather than a focused exam
Children and older adults are injured by less
A reassuring exam does not cancel the mechanism

teach.model_answer: A significant mechanism is one where the forces involved make serious internal injury plausible whether or not anything is visible. The usual list is falls from height, ejection, another occupant dying, rollover, high-speed collisions, penetrating injury to the head, neck, chest or abdomen, and pedestrians or cyclists struck by vehicles — confirm the exact thresholds in your text, because the numbers vary. What it changes is that you do a rapid scan of the whole body instead of a focused exam of what hurts. Children and older adults get badly hurt by much less, so the threshold drops for them. And the patient looking fine does not cancel it: mechanism raises suspicion, and a well-looking patient cannot talk you out of suspicion.

story.title: Walking and talking
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — vehicle into a tree, one occupant, patient out of the car.
story.body:
He met you at the roadside. Walking, embarrassed, saying he was fine and asking whether he really needed to go.

The car was off the road, front end folded, windscreen starred from the inside, and the driver's seat had come off its runners.

You did the rapid scan anyway, because of the car and not because of him. His abdomen was tender in a way he had not mentioned and did not seem to think mattered.

concepts.title: General impression
key_points: Formed in the first few seconds, from the doorway, before you touch the patient
You are answering one question: sick or not sick?
Built from appearance, work of breathing and skin colour
It sets the pace of everything that follows, not the diagnosis
A bad general impression justifies calling for help before you have any numbers
misconceptions: Waiting for vital signs before deciding how sick someone is
Treating the general impression as a diagnosis
Ignoring an instinct that something is wrong because the numbers look acceptable
exam_favorites: Sick or not sick in the first seconds
The three things it is built from
That it sets pace, not diagnosis

read.plain:
Before you kneel, before you touch anything, you look. The general impression is what you form in the first few seconds from the doorway, and it answers exactly one question: is this patient sick or not sick?

Three things build it. Appearance — are they alert, are they interacting, is their posture normal or are they rigid, slumped, tripoding. Work of breathing — is breathing effortless, or are they using muscles they should not need. And skin colour — pink, or grey, mottled, blue, sheet-white.

That is enough to decide how fast the next ten minutes are going to move. It is not a diagnosis and it is not meant to be. A patient who looks sick gets a faster, shorter, more aggressive assessment and an earlier call for help. A patient who looks well gets a more thorough, more leisurely one.

The part people undervalue is that this impression is allowed to override numbers. If someone looks terrible and their first set of vitals is unremarkable, believe your eyes and keep looking. Vital signs are a lagging indicator; appearance is not.
read.standard: The general impression is formed within the initial seconds of patient contact, prior to physical examination, and is used to categorise the patient as critically ill or not. It is derived from appearance including mentation and posture, work of breathing, and skin colour. Its function is to determine the urgency and depth of subsequent assessment and the timing of requests for additional resources, rather than to establish a diagnosis. Because compensatory mechanisms may maintain vital signs within normal limits in a deteriorating patient, an impression of critical illness is not invalidated by an initially reassuring set of vitals.

eli_new.analogy: You know within a second whether a room smells of smoke. You do not need a sensor to start moving.
eli_new.body: Experienced clinicians look sideways at a patient and know. What they are doing is not mystical: they are reading posture, effort and colour, all at once, faster than they can describe. You can learn it by naming those three things deliberately until it becomes automatic.

teach.prompt: Explain what the general impression is, what it is built from, and what it is for.

must_hit.point: Formed in the first seconds, before touching the patient
Answers sick or not sick
Built from appearance, work of breathing and skin colour
Sets pace, not diagnosis

teach.model_answer: It is what you form from the doorway in the first few seconds, before you touch anyone, and it answers one question: sick or not sick. You build it from three things — appearance, including mentation and posture, work of breathing, and skin colour. Its job is to set the pace and depth of everything that follows and to decide whether you call for help now, not to make a diagnosis. And it is allowed to beat the numbers: if someone looks terrible with an unremarkable first set of vitals, believe your eyes, because vitals lag and appearance does not.

story.title: From the doorway
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — 54-year-old male, feeling unwell, private residence.
story.body:
Called in as feeling unwell, which could be anything.

You got three steps into the room and stopped. He was upright, grey, silent, and breathing with his shoulders.

His first blood pressure was fine. Your partner called for ALS anyway, on the strength of what the room looked like. By the time they arrived the blood pressure had caught up with the impression.

concepts.title: Level of consciousness: AVPU and an introduction to GCS
key_points: AVPU is the rapid scale used in the primary assessment: Alert, responds to Verbal, responds to Painful, Unresponsive
Alert is further described by what the patient is orientated to — person, place, time and event
Responds to Verbal means they react to your voice, even if only by opening their eyes
Responds to Painful means they react only to a painful stimulus
Unresponsive means no response to any stimulus
The Glasgow Coma Scale scores eye opening, verbal response and motor response separately, and is more detailed than the primary assessment needs
What matters most is the trend: a level of consciousness that is falling is an emergency regardless of where it started
misconceptions: Recording a single AVPU value and never repeating it
Confusing 'alert' with 'orientated'
Using a painful stimulus before trying voice
exam_favorites: That the trend matters more than the value

read.plain:
In the primary assessment you need a level of consciousness fast, and AVPU is the tool. Four levels: Alert, responds to Verbal stimulus, responds to Painful stimulus, Unresponsive.

Alert means their eyes are open and they are interacting with you spontaneously. It does not automatically mean they know what is going on, which is why alert is usually qualified by what they are orientated to: person, place, time and event. Someone can be wide awake and have no idea what year it is.

Verbal means they were not spontaneously interacting but they respond to your voice — even just opening their eyes when you speak. Painful means voice does nothing and they respond only to a painful stimulus. Unresponsive means nothing produces a response at all.

Work down the scale in order. Speak before you touch, and touch before you cause pain.

The Glasgow Coma Scale is the more detailed version, scoring eye opening, verbal response and motor response separately and adding them up. You will meet it constantly; it is more granular than the primary assessment needs, and this is the introduction rather than the whole of it.

The single most useful thing about level of consciousness is not the value, it is the direction. A patient who was alert and is now responding only to voice is deteriorating, and that matters far more than any particular letter.
read.standard: Level of consciousness in the primary assessment is assessed using the AVPU scale: Alert, responsive to Verbal stimulus, responsive to Painful stimulus, Unresponsive. Alertness is qualified by orientation to person, place, time and event, as spontaneous eye opening and interaction do not establish orientation. Assessment proceeds hierarchically, with verbal stimulus applied before painful stimulus. The Glasgow Coma Scale provides a more granular assessment by scoring eye opening, verbal response and motor response independently and summing the components; it exceeds the granularity required for the primary assessment and is introduced here rather than treated in full. Serial assessment is more informative than any single value, and a declining level of consciousness constitutes a time-critical finding irrespective of the initial level.

eli_new.analogy: AVPU is four rungs on a ladder. Which rung matters less than which way they are moving.
eli_new.body: The four letters are easy. The thing that catches people is treating it as a label you write once. Level of consciousness is a measurement, and like any measurement it is nearly useless as a single reading and very powerful as a series.

teach.prompt: Explain the AVPU scale, how 'alert' is qualified, and why the trend matters more than the value.

must_hit.point: Alert, Verbal, Painful, Unresponsive
Alert is qualified by orientation to person, place, time, event

A falling level of consciousness is an emergency

teach.model_answer: AVPU is Alert, responds to Verbal, responds to Painful, Unresponsive. Alert means eyes open and interacting spontaneously, which is not the same as orientated — you qualify it by what they know: person, place, time and event. Work down in order, speaking before you touch and touching before you cause pain. The Glasgow Coma Scale is the more detailed version, scoring eye opening, verbal and motor separately, and it is more than the primary assessment needs. The most useful thing is the direction: a patient who was alert and now only answers to voice is deteriorating, and that matters more than any single letter.

story.title: Two letters in ten minutes
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — fall, elderly female, head injury.
story.body:
On arrival she was alert and cross about the fuss, orientated to everything you asked.

Ten minutes later, in the back of the truck, she answered you but only after you said her name twice, and she had stopped being cross.

Nothing about her blood pressure had changed. The letter had, and that was the finding you called ahead with.

concepts.title: Airway assessment in the primary survey
key_points: The question is not 'is there an airway' but 'is it open and will it stay open'
A patient speaking clearly in full sentences has a patent airway right now
Snoring, gurgling, stridor and silence are all airway findings, and silence is the worst of them
An airway that is open now can close: consider level of consciousness, swelling, bleeding and vomiting
You fix what you find before moving on — positioning, suction, adjunct — you do not note it and continue
misconceptions: Moving on to breathing with a noisy airway unaddressed
Treating a patient who is talking as having a permanently secure airway
Assuming a quiet airway is a clear airway
exam_favorites: That talking equals patent, for now

read.plain:
Airway is the first thing you can actually treat, and the rule of the primary assessment is that you deal with what you find before you move on.

The quickest test is speech. A patient who is talking to you in clear full sentences has a patent airway at this moment, and you can move on. That word 'moment' is doing a lot of work, because airways close.

When they are not talking, listen. Snoring is the tongue. Gurgling is fluid, and it means suction. Stridor is a high-pitched sound on breathing in and means upper airway narrowing, which is serious. And silence, in a patient who is clearly trying to breathe, is the most alarming finding of all, because it means nothing is moving.

Then think forwards. This airway is open now; will it stay open? A falling level of consciousness, swelling from a burn or an allergic reaction, blood in the mouth, active vomiting — all of these predict an airway that will close while you are still working.

And whatever you find, you fix it here. Reposition. Suction. Put in an adjunct. You do not write down 'noisy airway' and proceed to breathing.
read.standard: Airway assessment within the primary survey establishes both current patency and the likelihood of continued patency. A patient producing clear speech in complete sentences demonstrates a patent airway at that moment. In the absence of speech, auscultatory findings guide intervention: snoring indicates tongue-related obstruction, gurgling indicates fluid requiring suction, stridor indicates upper airway narrowing, and absent sound in a patient with visible respiratory effort indicates minimal or absent air movement and is the most concerning finding. Anticipated compromise is assessed by considering declining level of consciousness, airway oedema, hemorrhage and active vomiting. Identified airway compromise is corrected before the assessment proceeds.

eli_new.analogy: A door that is open now is not the same as a door that will stay open. Check the hinge as well as the gap.
eli_new.body: It is tempting to treat airway as a yes-or-no box. It is really two questions asked together: is air moving right now, and is anything about this patient going to stop it moving in the next ten minutes.

teach.prompt: Explain how you assess the airway in the primary survey and what the different sounds tell you.

must_hit.point: Clear speech in full sentences means patent now
Snoring is the tongue; gurgling means suction; stridor is upper airway narrowing
Silence with effort is the worst finding
Consider whether it will stay open
Fix it before moving on

teach.model_answer: You are asking two things: is it open now, and will it stay open. Clear speech in full sentences answers the first — that airway is patent at this moment. If they are not talking, listen: snoring is the tongue, gurgling means fluid and therefore suction, stridor is upper airway narrowing and is serious, and silence in someone visibly trying to breathe is the worst of all because nothing is moving. Then think ahead about a falling level of consciousness, swelling, blood or vomiting, any of which will close an airway that is open now. And whatever you find, you fix it here — reposition, suction, adjunct — before you move on to breathing.

story.title: He was talking a minute ago
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — allergic reaction, 30-year-old female, restaurant.
story.body:
She was talking when you arrived. Full sentences, anxious, complaining her throat felt tight.

You wrote 'airway patent'. Four minutes later her voice had changed, and a minute after that there was a high-pitched sound on every breath in.

Airway patent had been true. It had also been temporary, and the second question was the one that mattered.

concepts.title: Breathing assessment in the primary survey
key_points: You are looking for adequacy, not just presence: rate, depth and effort together
Look at the chest, listen for air movement, feel for it if you need to
Inadequate breathing is treated here with ventilation, not noted for later
Rate alone is misleading: fast and shallow can move less air than slow and deep
Agonal gasps are not breathing and must not be mistaken for it
misconceptions: Counting a rate and calling that the breathing assessment
Mistaking agonal gasps for adequate breathing
Deferring ventilation until after the rest of the survey

read.plain:
Breathing in the primary assessment is not a yes-or-no question either. Plenty of dying patients are breathing. The question is whether the breathing is adequate.

Three things together: rate, depth and effort. A rate on its own is misleading, and this is the trap that catches new EMTs. A patient breathing thirty times a minute with barely any chest movement may be moving far less useful air than one breathing twelve times deeply. Look at the chest rather than only counting.

Effort is the other half. Accessory muscles in the neck, retractions between the ribs, nasal flaring in a child, a patient who cannot say more than a few words at a time — all of these say that breathing is costing far more than it should.

One specific thing to recognise: agonal gasps. Slow, irregular, gulping movements in a patient who is otherwise not responsive. They look like breathing and they are not. A patient making agonal gasps is in cardiac arrest until proven otherwise.

And as with airway, inadequate breathing is treated at this point. You do not finish the survey first.
read.standard: Breathing assessment in the primary survey evaluates adequacy rather than presence, integrating rate, tidal volume and work of breathing. Respiratory rate considered in isolation is unreliable, as rapid shallow respiration may produce lower effective alveolar ventilation than slower respiration with adequate tidal volume. Increased work of breathing is indicated by accessory muscle use, intercostal or suprasternal retraction, nasal flaring in pediatric patients and inability to speak in complete sentences. Agonal respirations — slow, irregular, gasping movements in an unresponsive patient — do not constitute effective breathing and should be treated as indicating cardiac arrest. Inadequate ventilation identified at this stage is corrected immediately with positive-pressure ventilation before assessment continues.

eli_new.analogy: Counting breaths without watching the chest is like counting footsteps to work out how far someone walked, without checking the size of their steps.
eli_new.body: The number is the easy part and it is the least informative part. Two patients can breathe at the same rate and one of them is fine while the other is dying, and the only way to tell is to look at how much chest is actually moving and how hard they are working for it.

teach.prompt: Explain how you assess breathing in the primary survey and why the rate alone is not enough.

must_hit.point: Rate, depth and effort together
Fast and shallow can move less air than slow and deep
Agonal gasps are not breathing
Treat inadequate breathing here

teach.model_answer: You are assessing adequacy, not presence, which means rate, depth and effort together. Rate on its own misleads: thirty shallow breaths a minute can move less useful air than twelve deep ones, so look at the chest instead of only counting. Effort tells you the other half — accessory muscles, retractions, nasal flaring in a child, someone who can only manage a few words at a time. Recognise agonal gasps specifically: slow irregular gulping in an unresponsive patient is not breathing, and that patient is in cardiac arrest until proven otherwise. And inadequate breathing gets ventilated right here, not noted for later.

story.title: It looked like breathing
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — unresponsive male, bystanders on scene.
story.body:
The caller told dispatch he was still breathing, and from the doorway it looked like it — occasional big gulping movements, maybe four or five a minute.

Your partner checked a pulse while you watched the chest. There was no pulse, and those gulps were agonal.

Compressions started about eleven seconds after you came through the door, because nobody stopped to argue about whether that counted as breathing.

concepts.title: Circulation: pulse, bleeding and skin
key_points: Three things: a pulse, any major bleeding, and what the skin tells you
Check a central pulse in an unresponsive patient; a radial pulse in a responsive one
Major external bleeding is controlled at this point, immediately
Skin is assessed for colour, temperature and condition — colour, temperature, condition, often shortened to CTC
Cool, pale, clammy skin is the body shunting blood away from the surface, and is an early sign of shock
Skin findings often change before blood pressure does
misconceptions: Waiting for a blood pressure before suspecting shock
Assessing skin only by colour and ignoring temperature and moisture
Leaving major bleeding until after the survey

read.plain:
Circulation in the primary assessment is three quick things, and none of them require equipment.

First, is there a pulse. In an unresponsive patient, go central — the carotid — because peripheral pulses disappear early when perfusion drops. In a responsive patient the radial pulse is enough, and its presence tells you something about perfusion by itself.

Second, is there major bleeding. If there is, control it now. Not after the survey.

Third, the skin, and this is the part people undervalue. Three things: colour, temperature and condition. Pink, warm and dry is what you want. Pale, cool and clammy means the body is pulling blood away from the surface to protect the core, and that is a compensating patient — someone whose blood pressure has not fallen yet precisely because their body is working hard to stop it falling.

That is why skin matters so much. Blood pressure is a late sign. By the time it drops, the compensation has failed. Skin tells you earlier, and it tells you without a cuff.
read.standard: Circulatory assessment in the primary survey comprises pulse assessment, identification and control of major hemorrhage, and evaluation of skin. Pulse is assessed centrally at the carotid in unresponsive patients, as peripheral pulses are lost early in hypoperfusion, and radially in responsive patients. Major external hemorrhage is controlled at the point of identification. Skin is evaluated for colour, temperature and condition: pallor with cool, diaphoretic skin reflects peripheral vasoconstriction and sympathetic activation, representing compensated shock. Because blood pressure is maintained by compensatory mechanisms until they fail, cutaneous findings frequently precede measurable hypotension and are therefore an earlier indicator of hypoperfusion.

eli_new.analogy: The body turns off the lights in the outer rooms to keep the heating on in the middle of the house.
eli_new.body: Skin is the cheapest monitor you own. Cool, pale and sweaty means the body has decided the skin is expendable and is defending the organs that are not. That decision happens well before the blood pressure gives way.

teach.prompt: Explain the three parts of the circulation check and why skin findings matter so much.

must_hit.point: Pulse — carotid if unresponsive, radial if responsive
Control major bleeding immediately
Skin: colour, temperature, condition
Skin changes before blood pressure falls

teach.model_answer: Three things, none needing equipment. A pulse — carotid in an unresponsive patient because peripheral pulses go early, radial in a responsive one. Major external bleeding, which you control right there rather than after the survey. And the skin: colour, temperature and condition. Pink, warm and dry is normal; pale, cool and clammy means the body is shunting blood from the surface to protect the core. That matters because blood pressure is a late sign — it holds until compensation fails — so skin tells you a patient is in trouble before any cuff will.

story.title: Pressure was fine
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — motorcycle down, single rider, conscious.
story.body:
He was talking, his blood pressure was normal, and the new EMT was visibly relaxing.

His skin was grey, cold and wet, and his radial pulse was fast and thin under your fingers.

The pressure was normal because he was young and his body was working extremely hard to keep it there. It stayed normal for another eight minutes, and then it did not.

expansion: Colour — pink, pale, flushed, cyanotic, mottled, jaundiced
Temperature — warm, cool, cold, hot
Condition — dry, moist, clammy, diaphoretic
mnemonic.memory_image: Three words you can check with the back of one hand, faster than you can find a cuff.

concepts.title: The transport priority decision
key_points: The end of the primary assessment is a decision, not a summary
High priority means the patient goes now, with further assessment done on the way
Drivers of high priority include a poor general impression, an airway or breathing problem, uncontrolled bleeding, shock, an altered or falling level of consciousness, and severe pain
Priority decides pace and destination, and it can be revised in either direction
Deciding late costs the patient time that cannot be recovered
misconceptions: Finishing a full assessment on scene before deciding priority
Treating the priority decision as unchangeable once made
Downgrading a priority because the patient is now more comfortable
exam_favorites: That the primary assessment ends in a decision

read.plain:
The primary assessment does not end with a list of findings. It ends with a decision: does this patient go now, or do we have time?

High priority means the patient is loaded and further assessment happens on the move. The things that put someone in that category are the ones you have just been looking for — a general impression of a sick patient, an airway you are struggling to keep open, breathing that is inadequate, bleeding you have not controlled, signs of shock, a level of consciousness that is altered or falling, and severe pain.

That decision changes two things: how fast you move, and sometimes where you go.

It is also reversible. A patient who looked terrible and has improved with oxygen and positioning can be downgraded. A patient who looked stable and is quietly deteriorating gets upgraded — and that upgrade is the more important of the two, because it is the one people miss.

The cost of deciding late is the part to internalise. Everything you do on scene is time the patient is not in the place that can fix them. Deciding early is not being hasty; it is giving the hospital the minutes it needs.
read.standard: The primary assessment concludes with a transport priority determination rather than a summary of findings. High-priority designation indicates immediate transport with continued assessment performed en route. Indications include a general impression of critical illness, compromised or threatened airway, inadequate ventilation, uncontrolled hemorrhage, signs of hypoperfusion, altered or declining level of consciousness, and severe pain. The determination governs both the pace of on-scene activity and, where systems permit, destination selection. Priority is subject to revision in either direction on reassessment, with upgrade of an initially stable patient representing the more commonly missed change. Delayed determination consumes time that cannot be recovered downstream.

eli_new.analogy: The primary assessment is not a report. It is a question with two answers: now, or not now.
eli_new.body: It is easy to treat assessment as information-gathering that ends when you run out of things to check. The point of the primary survey is narrower than that: find the things that kill people quickly, fix what you can, and decide whether this patient can afford for you to stay.

teach.prompt: Explain what the primary assessment ends with and what would make a patient high priority.

must_hit.point: It ends in a transport priority decision
High priority means go now, assess en route
Drivers: bad impression, airway, breathing, bleeding, shock, altered LOC, severe pain
It can be revised in either direction

teach.model_answer: It ends with a decision, not a summary: does this patient go now or do we have time? High priority means you load and keep assessing on the way. The drivers are exactly what you have been looking for — a general impression of a sick patient, an airway you are fighting to hold, inadequate breathing, uncontrolled bleeding, signs of shock, an altered or falling level of consciousness, and severe pain. It changes your pace and sometimes your destination, and it can be revised either way — the upgrade of a patient who looked stable and is quietly deteriorating is the one people miss. Deciding late costs time nobody can get back.

story.title: Eleven minutes on a driveway
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — 71-year-old male, weakness, no other detail.
story.body:
He was grey and quiet and his skin was wet, and the crew did a careful, thorough, complete assessment on the driveway because nothing was obviously broken.

Eleven minutes. A full set of vitals, a second set, a history, a medication list.

None of it was wrong. All of it could have been done in the back of a moving ambulance, and the decision to go could have been made in the first ninety seconds.

concepts.title: XABC: life-threatening bleeding first
key_points: The traditional order is Airway, Breathing, Circulation
XABC puts eXsanguinating haemorrhage before the airway, because massive external bleeding kills faster than anything else
It applies where there is obvious, catastrophic external bleeding — an arterial bleed or an amputation
In practice it takes seconds: apply the tourniquet or the pressure, then go straight to airway
It does not replace ABC for every patient; it reorders it for the ones actively bleeding out
The change reflects what actually kills trauma patients in the first minutes
misconceptions: Applying XABC to every patient regardless of bleeding
Working through airway and breathing while a patient bleeds out from a limb
Believing XABC abandons the airway
exam_favorites: That it reorders rather than replaces ABC

read.plain:
The order you were taught is Airway, Breathing, Circulation, and it is right for the overwhelming majority of patients. Airway problems kill in minutes, breathing problems in a few more, circulation problems more slowly still.

There is one exception, and it comes from what people actually die of in the first minutes of major trauma. A patient with an arterial bleed from a limb, or a traumatic amputation, can lose a fatal volume of blood in less time than it takes to work carefully through an airway assessment. For that patient the order becomes XABC, where X stands for exsanguinating haemorrhage.

In practice this is not a philosophical reordering, it is a few seconds. You see the bleeding, you put a tourniquet on it or you put hard pressure on it, and then you go straight into the airway as normal. The X is not a new assessment phase; it is a single intervention inserted at the front.

And it applies only where the bleeding is obvious and catastrophic. A patient with a bleeding scalp wound gets ABC, and their bleeding gets dealt with at C.

What XABC really encodes is a piece of hard-won evidence: for the bleeding trauma patient, the clock on blood loss is faster than the clock on everything else.
read.standard: The conventional primary assessment sequence prioritises airway, breathing and circulation according to the rapidity with which each causes death. XABC modifies this sequence by placing control of exsanguinating external hemorrhage before airway assessment, reflecting evidence that massive external hemorrhage from extremity arterial injury or traumatic amputation produces death more rapidly than airway compromise in this specific population. The modification is procedural rather than structural: hemorrhage control is applied as a single immediate intervention — typically tourniquet application or direct pressure — after which the standard sequence proceeds. It is indicated only where catastrophic external hemorrhage is evident, and does not supersede the conventional sequence for other presentations.

eli_new.analogy: The order is set by which clock runs fastest. For a patient bleeding out of a limb, that clock is the blood.
eli_new.body: ABC is not a ritual, it is a ranking by how quickly each thing kills. XABC is the same logic applied honestly: when someone is losing blood at arterial speed, blood is now the fastest clock in the room, so it goes first.

teach.prompt: Explain what the X in XABC stands for, when you would use it, and why the order changes.

must_hit.point: X is exsanguinating or massive external haemorrhage
Used where bleeding is obvious and catastrophic
It is one immediate intervention, then straight to airway
It reorders rather than replaces ABC

teach.model_answer: The X is exsanguinating haemorrhage — massive external bleeding. ABC ranks things by how quickly they kill, and for most patients airway is the fastest clock. But a patient with an arterial limb bleed or a traumatic amputation can lose a fatal volume faster than you can work carefully through an airway, so for them blood becomes the fastest clock and goes first. In practice it takes seconds: tourniquet or hard pressure, then straight into airway as normal. It applies only where the bleeding is obvious and catastrophic — a bleeding scalp wound is still handled at C — so it reorders the sequence for a specific patient rather than replacing it for everyone.

story.title: Six seconds
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — industrial accident, arm injury, heavy bleeding reported.
story.body:
You could see it from the door: bright blood, pulsing, pooling out from under his left arm and a co-worker holding a jacket against it that was already soaked.

Nobody assessed an airway. Your partner had a tourniquet high on that arm and wound down inside about six seconds, and only then knelt at his head and started talking to him.

He was talking back. The airway had been fine the whole time. The blood had not.

concepts.title: SAMPLE history
key_points: SAMPLE is the framework for the history of every patient, medical or trauma
Signs and symptoms — what you can observe, and what the patient reports
Allergies — to medications, foods and environment
Medications — prescribed, over the counter, and anything else taken
Past medical history — relevant conditions, surgery and hospital admissions
Last oral intake — what and when, which matters for surgery and for diabetic patients
Events leading up — what was happening immediately before this started
The E is the one most often rushed and is frequently the most useful letter
misconceptions: Reciting the letters without listening to the answers
Taking the medication list only from what the patient remembers, when the bottles are on the table
Skipping last oral intake because it sounds irrelevant
exam_favorites: That it applies to trauma patients too

read.plain:
SAMPLE is the history you take on everyone. It is deliberately broad, because at the point you are asking you usually do not know what is wrong.

Signs and symptoms is the split between what you can see and measure and what the patient tells you. Allergies covers medications, foods and environment, and is worth asking even when it seems irrelevant. Medications means everything — prescribed, bought over the counter, borrowed, herbal. The most efficient version of this question is not asking; it is collecting the bottles.

Past medical history is the conditions, surgeries and admissions that bear on today. Last oral intake is what and when, which matters if they might go to surgery and matters enormously in a diabetic patient.

Events leading up is the letter people rush, and it is very often the one that solves the call. What exactly were you doing when this started? The answer separates chest pain at rest from chest pain climbing stairs, and it is the question that finds the seizure behind the crash.

And it is not only for medical patients. A trauma patient has a SAMPLE history too, and their medications and past history change how they respond to injury.
read.standard: The SAMPLE mnemonic structures history acquisition for all patients regardless of presentation: Signs and symptoms, Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last oral intake, and Events leading up to the incident. Signs are objectively observable findings while symptoms are subjectively reported. Medication histories are most reliably obtained by direct inspection of containers rather than patient recall. Last oral intake informs surgical planning and is of particular significance in diabetic patients. The events preceding onset frequently provide the diagnostically decisive information and are commonly under-explored. SAMPLE applies to trauma presentations as well as medical, as comorbidity and medication influence physiological response to injury.

eli_new.analogy: Six questions that fit in your pocket and work on a patient you know nothing about.
eli_new.body: The reason the same six questions are used on everybody is that at the moment you ask them, you usually do not yet know what is wrong. A framework that only works once you know the answer is not much of a framework.

teach.prompt: Run through SAMPLE and say which letter people most often rush, and why it matters.

must_hit.point: Signs and symptoms, Allergies, Medications, Past history, Last intake, Events
Events leading up is the one most often rushed
Medications are best collected, not recalled
It applies to trauma patients too

teach.model_answer: Signs and symptoms, Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last oral intake, and Events leading up. Signs are what you can see and measure, symptoms are what they report. For medications, collect the bottles rather than relying on memory. Last oral intake matters for surgery and for diabetic patients. The letter people rush is Events — what exactly were you doing when this started — and it is very often the one that solves the call, separating chest pain at rest from chest pain on exertion, or finding the seizure behind a crash. It applies to trauma patients too, because their medications and history change how they respond to injury.

story.title: The last letter
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — 58-year-old male, chest pain, at home.
story.body:
Everything about the history was unremarkable until the last question.

What were you doing when it started? He had been carrying a washing machine up a flight of stairs with his son.

That single answer changed the whole shape of the call, and it was the one the crew nearly skipped because they already had the other five letters.

Allergies — medications, foods, environment
Medications — prescribed, over the counter, anything taken (collect the bottles)
Past medical history — conditions, surgery, admissions
Last oral intake — what and when
Events leading up — what was happening when it started
mnemonic.memory_image: Six questions in your pocket that work on a patient you know nothing about. The last one usually solves it.

concepts.title: OPQRST
key_points: OPQRST interrogates a symptom, usually pain, in detail
Onset — what were they doing, and did it start suddenly or gradually
Provocation and palliation — what makes it worse and what makes it better
Quality — the patient's own words for what it feels like
Region and radiation — where it is and where it travels
Severity — a scale, mainly useful for comparison over time
Time — how long it has been going on, and whether it has happened before
Quality is recorded in the patient's words, not translated into yours
misconceptions: Putting words in the patient's mouth when asking about quality
Treating a severity score as an objective measurement
Using OPQRST instead of SAMPLE rather than alongside it

read.plain:
Where SAMPLE describes the patient, OPQRST describes the complaint. They are companions, not alternatives: SAMPLE is the person, OPQRST is the pain.

Onset asks what they were doing and whether it arrived suddenly or crept up. Provocation and palliation asks what makes it worse and what makes it better — movement, breathing, position, rest, medication. Quality asks what it feels like, and the discipline here is to record their words. If they say it feels like a band around the chest, write that down. Do not offer them a menu of adjectives and then write down the one they picked.

Region and radiation asks where it is and where it goes. Severity asks for a number, and the number matters far less than people think in absolute terms — its value is comparison. A seven now and a nine in ten minutes tells you something; a seven on its own tells you very little.

Time asks how long, and it is worth adding: has this ever happened before, and was it like this?

Used together, these two frameworks give you a person and a problem, which is most of what a receiving clinician needs from you.
read.standard: OPQRST provides systematic interrogation of a symptom, most commonly pain: Onset, Provocation and palliation, Quality, Region and radiation, Severity, and Time. Onset establishes activity at the time of symptom initiation and whether onset was abrupt or gradual. Provocation and palliation identify exacerbating and relieving factors. Quality should be documented using the patient's own descriptive language rather than clinician-supplied terminology, as leading questions compromise the diagnostic value of the response. Region and radiation establish location and referral pattern. Severity, typically elicited as a numerical rating, derives its principal value from serial comparison rather than absolute magnitude. Time establishes duration and prior occurrence. OPQRST complements rather than replaces SAMPLE.

eli_new.analogy: SAMPLE is the person. OPQRST is the pain. You need both to tell the story.
eli_new.body: The commonest error is a leading question. If you ask whether the pain is crushing, a frightened patient will very often say yes, and you have just invented a finding. Ask what it feels like, then stop talking.

teach.prompt: Run through OPQRST and explain why quality must be recorded in the patient's own words.

must_hit.point: Onset, Provocation/palliation, Quality, Region/radiation, Severity, Time
Quality in the patient's own words, no leading questions
Severity is mainly for comparison over time
It complements SAMPLE rather than replacing it

teach.model_answer: Onset — what were they doing and did it come on suddenly or gradually. Provocation and palliation — what makes it worse and what makes it better. Quality — what it feels like, in their words. Region and radiation — where it is and where it travels. Severity — a number. Time — how long, and has it happened before. Quality goes down verbatim because a leading question invents findings: ask a frightened patient whether it is crushing and many will agree, and now that word is in the record. Severity matters mostly for comparison — a seven that becomes a nine is information, a seven on its own is not much. And it sits alongside SAMPLE, which describes the person rather than the pain.

story.title: In her own words
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — 63-year-old female, chest discomfort.
story.body:
The student asked whether the pain was crushing. She said yes, because that was the word on offer and she was frightened.

The paramedic asked her again, differently: what does it actually feel like? She thought about it and said it felt like indigestion, high up, and that it had been coming and going for two days.

Both answers went in the notes. Only one of them was hers.

expansion: Onset — what were you doing? sudden or gradual?
Provocation and palliation — what makes it worse? what makes it better?
Quality — what does it feel like? (their words, no menu)
Region and radiation — where is it? where does it go?
Severity — a number, mainly useful for comparison
Time — how long? has it happened before?

concepts.title: Chief complaint versus the primary problem
key_points: The chief complaint is what the patient says is wrong, in their words
The primary problem is what is actually threatening them, which may be different
The chief complaint is recorded as stated, not translated into a diagnosis
A patient may lead with the symptom that frightens them rather than the one that matters
Some patients lead with the least alarming complaint out of embarrassment or denial
misconceptions: Rewriting the chief complaint into medical language
Assuming the loudest complaint is the most dangerous one
Stopping the assessment once the stated complaint is explained
exam_favorites: Why patients lead with the wrong thing

read.plain:
The chief complaint is the answer to why did you call today, recorded in the patient's own words. Not your interpretation of it. If they say I feel funny, the chief complaint is that they feel funny.

The primary problem is what is actually threatening them, and the gap between the two is where patients get missed.

People lead with the symptom that frightens them, which is not reliably the dangerous one. Someone may complain bitterly about a grazed elbow and mention almost in passing that they blacked out before they fell. The elbow is the chief complaint. The syncope is the primary problem.

And some patients minimise. They lead with the least alarming thing on the list because they are embarrassed, or frightened of the answer, or do not want to make a fuss. Older patients in particular will apologise for calling while describing something serious.

So you record what they said, and you keep assessing past it. Explaining the chief complaint is not the same as finishing the call.
read.standard: The chief complaint is the patient's stated reason for seeking care, documented verbatim rather than translated into clinical terminology. The primary problem is the condition presenting the greatest threat, which may differ from the chief complaint. Patients commonly present the symptom producing the most alarm rather than the most clinically significant finding, and may minimise or omit significant symptoms through embarrassment, denial or reluctance to inconvenience responders. Assessment therefore continues beyond explanation of the stated complaint, and identification of a plausible cause for the chief complaint does not conclude the evaluation.

eli_new.analogy: What they called about and what is wrong with them are two different questions. Ask both.
eli_new.body: The chief complaint is the door the patient opened. It is not necessarily the room the problem is in, and walking through the door and stopping there is how serious things get missed.

teach.prompt: Explain the difference between the chief complaint and the primary problem, and why patients often lead with the wrong one.

must_hit.point: Chief complaint is what they say, in their words
Primary problem is what is actually threatening them
Patients lead with what frightens them or minimise out of embarrassment
Keep assessing past the stated complaint

teach.model_answer: The chief complaint is what the patient says is wrong, recorded in their words — if they say they feel funny, that is the chief complaint. The primary problem is what is actually threatening them, and the gap between the two is where people get missed. Patients lead with whatever frightens them most, which is not reliably the dangerous thing: someone may complain about a grazed elbow and mention in passing that they blacked out before falling. Others minimise out of embarrassment or a reluctance to be a nuisance, older patients especially. So you record what they said and keep assessing past it, because explaining the complaint is not the same as finishing the call.

story.title: The elbow
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — 74-year-old male, fall, minor injury.
story.body:
He wanted to talk about his elbow. It was grazed and it was bleeding a little and it clearly annoyed him a great deal.

It was only when your partner asked what happened just before he fell that he said, offhand, that everything had gone grey for a second.

Chief complaint: grazed elbow. Primary problem: syncope in a 74-year-old. He would not have mentioned the second one if nobody had asked.

concepts.title: Interviewing and difficult histories
key_points: Open questions first, closed questions to narrow down
Get to the patient's eye level and give them time to answer
Silence is a tool: people fill it with information
Avoid leading questions, which manufacture findings that were never there
Children, older adults, patients who are deaf or do not share your language, and intoxicated or frightened patients all need the approach adapted rather than abandoned
Family and bystanders are a legitimate source when the patient cannot tell you
Ask about sensitive subjects directly and without an audience
misconceptions: Interviewing a patient while standing over them
Asking leading questions to speed things up
Interviewing a teenager in front of their parents about sensitive topics
Giving up on a history because the patient is difficult to interview

read.plain:
A history is a conversation you are steering, and the quality of what you get back depends almost entirely on how you ask.

Start open. What is going on today? Tell me about it. Let them talk before you start narrowing. Then use closed questions to pin down what you still need. Doing it the other way round gives you a series of yes and no answers and no story.

Get down to their eye level. Somebody standing over you is someone you give short answers to. And leave silences alone; most people will fill them, and what they fill them with is often the thing they were not sure whether to mention.

Avoid leading. It is the single most damaging habit in history taking, because it does not merely waste time, it creates findings that were never there and then those findings get handed to the hospital.

Some histories are hard. A frightened child. An older patient who is hard of hearing. Someone who does not share your language. Someone intoxicated, or in pain, or convinced they are wasting your time. None of that is a reason to stop — it is a reason to change how you are asking. Use family. Use the bottles on the side. Use interpretation if you have it.

And the sensitive questions — drug use, pregnancy, domestic violence, self-harm — get asked directly, in plain language, and without an audience. A question you asked in front of somebody's partner may as well not have been asked.
read.standard: History acquisition is an interview technique. Open-ended questioning is used initially to elicit narrative, with closed questioning subsequently applied to clarify specific points; reversing this order yields a series of discrete answers without a coherent history. Positioning at the patient's eye level and tolerating silence improve disclosure. Leading questions should be avoided, as they generate findings that were not independently reported and that subsequently propagate into the clinical record. Communication barriers — pediatric and geriatric patients, hearing impairment, language discordance, intoxication and anxiety — require adaptation of technique rather than abandonment of the history, with family members and medication containers serving as legitimate collateral sources. Sensitive subjects are addressed directly and out of the hearing of accompanying persons.

eli_new.analogy: A leading question does not save you time. It just puts your words into the record with the patient's name on them.
eli_new.body: The instinct under time pressure is to ask fast closed questions, because they produce fast answers. They also produce a history with no shape, and they invite the patient to agree with whatever you suggested. Slowing down for the first thirty seconds usually saves time overall.

teach.prompt: Explain how you would take a history from a patient who is hard to interview, and what a leading question does.

must_hit.point: Open questions first, then closed
Eye level, time, and allow silence
Leading questions create findings that were never there
Adapt rather than abandon; use family and medication containers
Sensitive questions asked directly and privately

teach.model_answer: Start open — tell me what is going on — and let them talk before narrowing with closed questions; doing it the other way gives you yes-and-no answers and no story. Get to their eye level, give them time, and leave silences alone, because people fill them with the thing they were unsure about mentioning. Never lead: asking whether the pain is crushing manufactures a finding that then follows the patient into hospital. When the interview is hard — a frightened child, someone hard of hearing, no shared language, intoxication — you change the approach rather than give up, using family, the medication bottles, and interpretation. And ask the sensitive things directly and without an audience, because a question asked in front of someone's partner may as well not have been asked.

story.title: Wait four seconds
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — 17-year-old female, abdominal pain, at home with parents.
story.body:
Her answers in the living room were short and gave you nothing.

On the way to the ambulance, alone, your partner asked the same question and then said nothing at all for about four seconds.

She filled the silence. The history changed completely, and so did the destination.

concepts.title: Rapid full-body scan
key_points: Used for a patient with a significant mechanism of injury, an unresponsive patient, or one who is unstable
A fast, systematic sweep of the whole body looking for injuries you have not been told about
Works head to toe: head, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, extremities, then the back
You are looking and feeling for DCAP-BTLS findings at every region
Expose what you need to see, and protect the patient's dignity and temperature while you do it
It takes well under a couple of minutes; if it is taking longer you are doing a detailed exam instead
misconceptions: Performing a rapid scan on a patient with an isolated minor injury
Skipping the back because the patient is on a stretcher
Turning the scan into a slow detailed examination on scene

read.plain:
The rapid full-body scan is what you do when the mechanism tells you there may be injuries the patient has not mentioned and cannot feel. It is for the patient with a significant mechanism, the unresponsive patient, and the unstable one.

It is fast and it is systematic, and the system is what makes it fast. Head, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, extremities, and then the back. Always the same order, so you cannot skip a region by accident under pressure.

At each region you are looking and feeling for the same set of findings, which is what DCAP-BTLS collects. Your hands are doing as much work as your eyes: crepitus, instability and tenderness are felt rather than seen.

Expose what you need to expose to actually see an injury, because a hand on top of a jacket finds very little. Balance that against dignity and against heat loss, which is a real risk in a trauma patient.

And keep it rapid. This is a sweep for things that will kill the patient, not a catalogue of every bruise. If you are still on scene doing it several minutes later, you have drifted into a detailed exam and the patient is paying for it in time.
read.standard: The rapid full-body scan is indicated for patients with a significant mechanism of injury, unresponsive patients, and patients who are physiologically unstable. It comprises a rapid systematic survey of head, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, extremities and posterior surfaces, conducted in a fixed sequence to prevent omission under pressure. Each region is inspected and palpated for the findings collected by the DCAP-BTLS mnemonic, with palpation identifying crepitus, instability and tenderness not apparent on inspection. Adequate exposure is required for meaningful examination, balanced against patient dignity and prevention of hypothermia. The examination is intended to be completed rapidly; prolongation converts it into a detailed physical examination and delays definitive care.

eli_new.analogy: You are not cataloguing the damage. You are checking whether anything here is going to kill him in the next twenty minutes.
eli_new.body: The order exists so that you can be frightened, rushed and distracted and still not skip the pelvis. Under pressure, people do not improvise reliably; they fall back on whatever sequence they drilled.

teach.prompt: Explain who gets a rapid full-body scan, what order you work in, and what you are feeling for.

must_hit.point: Significant mechanism, unresponsive, or unstable patients
Head to toe in a fixed order, including the back
Looking and feeling for DCAP-BTLS findings
Expose enough to see, manage dignity and heat loss
Keep it fast

teach.model_answer: It is for a patient with a significant mechanism, an unresponsive patient, or an unstable one — anyone who may have injuries they have not told you about. You work head to toe in a fixed order: head, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, extremities, then the back, because a fixed order is what stops you skipping a region under pressure. At each region you look and you feel, checking for the DCAP-BTLS findings, and your hands find crepitus, instability and tenderness that your eyes cannot. Expose enough to actually see the injury, while managing dignity and heat loss. And keep it rapid — this is a sweep for what will kill them, not a catalogue of bruises.

story.title: The region nobody checked
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — fall from scaffolding, approximately four metres.
story.body:
The crew did a good scan. Head, neck, chest, abdomen, extremities. He was talking the whole time and nothing hurt except his wrist.

They did not log-roll him, because he was already on the board and it seemed unnecessary.

The hospital found the injury on his back within ten minutes of arrival. Nobody had looked at the one surface he could not see either.
