concepts.title: Focused assessment for the medical patient
key_points: Driven by the chief complaint and the history rather than by a mechanism
You examine the system the complaint points to, in depth, rather than sweeping everything
A responsive medical patient gives you the history first, and the history tells you where to look
It is focused, not brief: the examination of the relevant system should be thorough
If the picture does not fit the complaint, widen the examination
misconceptions: Performing a full trauma sweep on a responsive medical patient
Examining only the area the patient points at without examining the system
Ignoring findings that do not fit the working picture
exam_favorites: History first in a responsive medical patient
Widening when it does not fit

read.plain:
A responsive medical patient is assessed in the opposite direction to a trauma patient. With trauma, the mechanism tells you where to look. With a medical complaint, the history tells you, which means you take the history first and let it aim the examination.

So a patient complaining of difficulty breathing gets a thorough respiratory examination: work of breathing, chest movement, breath sounds in all the places you should listen, skin, position, ability to speak. A patient with chest pain gets that plus a careful look at everything that might be cardiac or vascular.

Focused does not mean quick and thin. It means aimed. The examination of the relevant system should be more thorough than it would be in a rapid sweep, not less.

And hold it loosely. If what you find does not match the story you were told, that is information. Widen out. A medical patient who does not add up may be a trauma patient who has not mentioned a fall, or a patient whose primary problem is not the one they led with.
read.standard: Assessment of the responsive medical patient is directed by the chief complaint and history rather than by mechanism of injury, and the history is therefore obtained before the physical examination. The examination focuses in depth on the body system implicated by the presenting complaint; focus denotes direction rather than brevity, and examination of the relevant system should exceed the depth achieved in a rapid survey. Findings inconsistent with the presenting history warrant broadening of the examination, as incongruent findings may indicate unreported trauma or a primary problem distinct from the stated complaint.

eli_new.analogy: Trauma: the mechanism points at the body. Medical: the story points at the body. Either way, something aims you.
eli_new.body: Focused is often misread as short. It is not — it means you are pointing the examination somewhere specific instead of sweeping. The respiratory exam on a breathless patient should be the most careful respiratory exam you do all shift.

teach.prompt: Explain how you assess a responsive medical patient and how that differs from a trauma patient.

must_hit.point: Driven by chief complaint and history, not mechanism
History first in a responsive medical patient
Focused means aimed and thorough, not brief
Widen if findings do not fit

teach.model_answer: With trauma the mechanism aims you; with a medical patient the history does, so in a responsive medical patient you take the history first and let it point the examination. Then you examine that system properly — a breathless patient gets a full respiratory exam, not a glance. Focused means aimed, not brief: the examination of the relevant system should be more thorough than anything in a rapid sweep, not less. And if what you find does not match what you were told, widen out, because that mismatch may mean unreported trauma or a primary problem that is not the complaint they led with.

story.title: It did not add up
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — 44-year-old male, difficulty breathing.
story.body:
The history was a respiratory one and the respiratory exam was unremarkable. Clear, equal, no work of breathing to speak of.

That mismatch is what made your partner widen out rather than accept it.

His abdomen was rigid. He had not mentioned falling off a ladder the previous evening, because he did not think it was related.

concepts.title: DCAP-BTLS
key_points: The checklist of findings you look and feel for at every region of a physical examination
Deformities — anything not the shape it should be
Contusions — bruising
Abrasions — scraped skin
Punctures and penetrations — holes
Burns
Tenderness — pain on palpation
Lacerations — cuts
Swelling
Half of these are found with your hands rather than your eyes
misconceptions: Looking for DCAP-BTLS findings without palpating
Applying it only to the area that hurts
Reciting the letters without applying them to each region
exam_favorites: That it is applied at every region
That tenderness is felt, not seen

read.plain:
DCAP-BTLS is not an assessment in its own right. It is the checklist of findings you are hunting for at every single region as you work through a physical examination, and its value is that it stops you looking only for the obvious.

Deformities: anything that is not the shape it should be. Contusions: bruising. Abrasions: scraped skin. Punctures or penetrations: holes, which are easy to miss in dark clothing and in hair. Burns. Tenderness: pain when you press, which you cannot see. Lacerations: cuts. Swelling.

Notice how many of those require hands. Tenderness is invisible. Deformity is often felt before it is seen. Swelling under clothing does not announce itself. An examination conducted entirely by eye finds perhaps half of what is there.

And it goes with every region, not just the one that hurts. The point of a systematic examination is the injuries the patient has not told you about, and those are by definition somewhere you were not already looking.
read.standard: DCAP-BTLS is a mnemonic enumerating the findings sought during physical examination of each body region: Deformities, Contusions, Abrasions, Punctures and penetrations, Burns, Tenderness, Lacerations and Swelling. It functions as a checklist applied region by region rather than as an independent assessment. Several findings — notably tenderness, deformity and subcutaneous swelling — are identified by palpation rather than inspection, and examination conducted by inspection alone detects a substantially reduced proportion of injuries. Application to all regions rather than to the symptomatic area alone is essential, as the purpose of systematic examination is identification of injuries not reported by the patient.

eli_new.analogy: Eight things to hunt for, at every stop along the body. Half of them are invisible.
eli_new.body: The commonest failure is not forgetting a letter, it is doing the whole examination with your eyes. Tenderness is the letter that catches people, because a patient who has not been pressed cannot tell you that pressing hurts.

teach.prompt: Say what DCAP-BTLS stands for and explain why you cannot do it by looking alone.

must_hit.point: Deformities, Contusions, Abrasions, Punctures/penetrations
Burns, Tenderness, Lacerations, Swelling
Tenderness and deformity are felt, not seen
Applied at every region, not only where it hurts

teach.model_answer: Deformities, Contusions, Abrasions, Punctures or penetrations, Burns, Tenderness, Lacerations and Swelling. It is a checklist of what you hunt for at each region rather than an assessment on its own. You cannot do it by eye because several of those findings are invisible — tenderness only exists once you press, deformity is often felt before it is seen, and swelling under clothing does not announce itself. And it is applied at every region, not just the painful one, because the whole purpose of a systematic examination is finding the injuries the patient has not mentioned.

story.title: Nothing to see
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — assault, male, conscious, no obvious injuries.
story.body:
Dark clothing, poor light, patient sitting up and insisting he was fine and did not want to go.

Nothing to see. Your partner ran hands over him anyway, region by region, and stopped at the left lower chest where the patient flinched hard.

There was a small puncture there, almost invisible against the fabric. Nobody was ever going to find that by looking.

expansion: Deformities — not the shape it should be
Contusions — bruising
Abrasions — scraped skin
Punctures and penetrations — holes, easily missed in dark clothing and hair
Burns
Tenderness — pain on palpation, which you cannot see
Lacerations — cuts
Swelling — often felt before it is seen

concepts.title: The detailed head-to-toe examination
key_points: A thorough, unhurried examination usually performed en route rather than on scene
Covers every region in order, including the areas already scanned
Includes findings that are not immediately life-threatening but still matter
Not every patient needs one: it is for patients whose injuries or condition justify it
It is the examination that finds the things the rapid scan was moving too fast to notice
misconceptions: Performing a detailed examination on scene while the patient deteriorates
Assuming the rapid scan already found everything
Performing it on every patient regardless of need
exam_favorites: When and where it is done
That it repeats regions already scanned

read.plain:
The detailed examination is the unhurried version, and the thing to understand about it is where it happens. It is usually done in the back of a moving ambulance, not on the pavement, because the patients who need it are usually patients who need to be moving.

It covers everything, in order, including regions the rapid scan already covered. That repetition is deliberate. A scan performed in ninety seconds on a noisy scene with a frightened patient misses things, and the detailed examination is your second look with better light, more time and less adrenaline.

It also picks up the findings that are real but not immediately lethal: the wrist that turns out to be broken, the small laceration hidden in the hairline, the tenderness nobody noticed while dealing with the chest.

And it is not universal. A patient with an isolated ankle injury and normal vital signs does not need their whole body examined in detail. Match it to the patient.
read.standard: The detailed physical examination is a comprehensive, unhurried regional examination typically performed during transport rather than on scene. It encompasses all body regions in sequence, including those previously assessed during the rapid full-body scan; repetition is deliberate, as the rapid scan is conducted under time pressure and in suboptimal conditions and is expected to miss findings. The detailed examination identifies injuries that are clinically significant but not immediately life-threatening. It is indicated selectively according to mechanism and patient condition rather than universally, and is not required for patients with isolated minor injury and normal physiology.

eli_new.analogy: The rapid scan is a torch swept across a room. The detailed exam is turning the lights on.
eli_new.body: People assume that if the rapid scan was done properly there is nothing left to find. The rapid scan was done in ninety seconds by someone with adrenaline in their bloodstream on a scene with poor light. A second, slower look is not redundancy.

teach.prompt: Explain what the detailed head-to-toe examination is, where it is usually done, and why it repeats what the rapid scan covered.

must_hit.point: Thorough and unhurried, usually en route
Covers all regions including ones already scanned
The rapid scan misses things under time pressure
Not every patient needs one

teach.model_answer: It is the thorough, unhurried version, and it is usually done in the back of a moving ambulance rather than on scene, because the patients who need it are the ones who need to be moving. It covers every region in order, including the ones the rapid scan already covered, and that repetition is deliberate — a ninety-second scan on a noisy scene with poor light and adrenaline misses things, so this is the second look with better conditions. It picks up what is real but not immediately lethal: the fractured wrist, the laceration in the hairline, tenderness nobody noticed. And it is selective: an isolated ankle injury with normal vitals does not need one.

story.title: Better light
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — motorcycle versus car, rider conscious.
story.body:
The scan on the road found the obvious things and nothing else, and everybody was focused on getting him off the carriageway.

In the back, with the lights on and the doors shut, the detailed exam found a deep laceration in his hairline that had been hidden by hair and by the dark.

It was not going to kill him. It was also not going to be found on that road.

concepts.title: Assessing the unresponsive medical patient
key_points: An unresponsive medical patient cannot give you a history, so you take one from everything else
They are assessed like a trauma patient: a rapid full-body scan, because they cannot tell you what hurts
The scene is a history: medication bottles, medical alert jewellery, oxygen equipment, the position they were found in
Family and bystanders become the history, and what they say about the last few hours matters most
Check a blood glucose in any patient with an altered level of consciousness
Consider trauma even when the call sounds medical, because an unresponsive patient may have fallen
misconceptions: Assuming an unresponsive patient with no obvious injury is purely medical
Failing to look around the room for the history
Omitting a blood glucose in an altered patient
exam_favorites: Scan them like a trauma patient

read.plain:
An unresponsive medical patient is the hardest history you will take, because the person who knows what happened cannot tell you.

So you assess them the way you assess a trauma patient: a rapid full-body scan. Not because you assume they are injured, but because they cannot tell you what hurts, and the usual method of finding out — asking — is unavailable.

Then you take the history from everything that is not the patient. The room is a history. Bottles on the side and in the bathroom cabinet. A medical alert bracelet. An oxygen concentrator in the corner. A glucometer on the table. The position they were found in, and whether anything looks disturbed.

Family and bystanders become your source, and the question that yields most is what the last few hours looked like. Not their whole medical history — what was different today.

Check a glucose. Any patient with an altered level of consciousness gets one, because hypoglycaemia is common, it mimics almost everything else, and it is one of the few causes an EMT can do something about.

And keep trauma on the table. An unresponsive patient found on the floor may have been unresponsive and then fallen, or fallen and then become unresponsive, and you cannot tell which from the doorway.
read.standard: The unresponsive medical patient cannot provide history, and assessment is adapted accordingly. A rapid full-body scan is performed, as the patient cannot localise symptoms and inspection and palpation substitute for subjective report. Environmental assessment provides collateral history: medication containers, medical identification jewellery, home oxygen or glucometry equipment, and the position in which the patient was found. Family and bystanders are questioned, with emphasis on events of the preceding hours rather than remote history. Blood glucose measurement is indicated in all patients with altered mental status, as hypoglycaemia is prevalent, mimics numerous other presentations, and is correctable at the EMT level. Traumatic injury must be considered, as unresponsiveness and falls occur in either causal order.

eli_new.analogy: The patient has lost their voice, so the room has to speak for them.
eli_new.body: Everything you normally rely on comes from asking. When asking is not available, the instinct is to feel stuck. The answer is that the information is still there, it is just distributed around the room and among the people standing in it.

teach.prompt: Explain how you assess an unresponsive medical patient when they cannot give you a history.

must_hit.point: Rapid full-body scan, because they cannot say what hurts
The scene is the history: bottles, jewellery, equipment, position found
Family and bystanders, focused on the last few hours
Check a blood glucose
Consider trauma as well

teach.model_answer: You assess them like a trauma patient, with a rapid full-body scan, not because you assume injury but because asking what hurts is unavailable and your hands have to replace it. Then you take the history from everything that is not the patient: medication bottles, a medical alert bracelet, home oxygen, a glucometer, the position they were found in. Family and bystanders become the source, and the most productive question is what the last few hours looked like rather than their whole history. Check a blood glucose on any altered patient, because hypoglycaemia is common, mimics nearly everything, and is one of the few things you can fix. And keep trauma in mind — they may have fallen, in either causal order.

story.title: The cabinet
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — unresponsive female, found by her son, no further information.
story.body:
She could not tell you anything. Her son had moved out years ago and did not know her medications.

Your partner opened the bathroom cabinet and photographed the shelf. Four bottles, one of them a diabetic medication, and a glucometer on the windowsill with a strip still in it.

Her blood sugar was low enough to explain everything. The history had been in the bathroom the whole time.

concepts.title: Pulse: rate, rhythm and quality
key_points: Three things every time: rate, rhythm and quality — a number alone is not a pulse assessment
Normal adult resting rate is 60 to 100 beats per minute
Rates are faster in children and faster still in infants, falling toward adult values with age
Rhythm is regular or irregular
Quality is strong, weak or thready — a thready pulse is a perfusion finding
Radial in a responsive patient, carotid in an unresponsive adult, brachial in an infant
A weak fast pulse with cool skin is a compensating patient, whatever the number says
misconceptions: Recording a rate and calling that the pulse
Using a carotid pulse routinely in a conscious patient
Treating a normal rate as reassurance when the pulse is thready

read.plain:
A pulse is three findings, not one. Rate, rhythm and quality — and the two that get skipped are the two that carry the most information.

Rate in a resting adult is normally 60 to 100. Children run faster, and infants faster again, with rates falling toward adult values as they grow. Take the exact pediatric bands from your text, because they differ between editions.

Rhythm is simply whether the beats are evenly spaced. Irregular is a finding worth reporting even when everything else looks fine.

Quality is what your fingers feel. Strong and full, or weak, or thready — thin and difficult to find. A thready pulse says the volume behind each beat is small, and that is a perfusion statement that a number cannot make.

Where you feel depends on the patient. Radial in a responsive adult. Carotid in an unresponsive adult, because peripheral pulses disappear early when perfusion falls. Brachial in an infant.

And put the three together. A pulse of 104 means very little on its own. A pulse of 104 that is thready, in a patient whose skin is cool and damp, is a patient compensating for something.
read.standard: Pulse assessment comprises rate, rhythm and quality. Normal resting adult rate is 60 to 100 beats per minute; pediatric rates are higher and decline toward adult values with increasing age, with specific age-band ranges varying between texts. Rhythm is characterised as regular or irregular. Quality is described as strong, weak or thready and reflects stroke volume and perfusion status. Assessment site is determined by age and responsiveness: radial in the responsive adult, carotid in the unresponsive adult owing to early loss of peripheral pulses in hypoperfusion, and brachial in the infant. Interpretation requires integration of all three components with other perfusion findings, as rate alone is a poor discriminator.

eli_new.analogy: A number tells you how often the pump is working. Quality tells you how much is coming out each time.
eli_new.body: New EMTs count and write the number down. The number is the least informative of the three findings. Whether each beat feels strong or barely there is what tells you how the patient is doing.

teach.prompt: Explain the three components of a pulse assessment and why the number alone is not enough.

must_hit.point: Rate, rhythm and quality
Normal adult 60 to 100
Site: radial responsive, carotid unresponsive, brachial infant
A thready pulse is a perfusion finding

teach.model_answer: Rate, rhythm and quality, every time. Normal resting adult rate is 60 to 100; children are faster and infants faster still, falling toward adult values with age. Rhythm is just whether the beats are evenly spaced, and irregular is worth reporting. Quality is what your fingers feel — strong, weak, or thready — and a thready pulse says there is little volume behind each beat, which is a perfusion statement a number cannot make. Radial in a responsive adult, carotid in an unresponsive one because peripheral pulses go early, brachial in an infant. A rate of 104 means little; 104 and thready with cool damp skin is a compensating patient.

story.title: A hundred and four
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — 26-year-old female, abdominal pain.
story.body:
Her pulse was 104, which the student wrote down and moved past because it was only just outside the range.

The paramedic put two fingers on the same wrist and said one word: thready.

It was the quality, not the rate, that made her a different patient. The number had been almost normal right up until it was not.

concepts.title: Respirations: rate and quality
key_points: Rate and quality together, the same way a pulse needs more than a number
Normal adult resting rate is 12 to 20 breaths per minute
Children breathe faster, infants faster still, falling toward adult values with age
Quality covers depth, effort and sound: normal, shallow, laboured, noisy
Count without telling the patient you are counting, because being watched changes the rate
A rate inside the normal range with shallow depth and heavy effort is not a normal respiratory assessment
misconceptions: Counting a rate and recording nothing about quality
Announcing that you are counting respirations
Treating a normal rate as a normal respiratory status

read.plain:
Respirations are assessed the same way as a pulse: a number plus a description, and the description is where the information lives.

A resting adult normally breathes 12 to 20 times a minute. Children are faster and infants faster again, falling toward adult figures as they grow; take the exact bands from your text.

Quality means depth, effort and sound. Is the chest moving normally or barely? Are they using muscles they should not need? Is there a noise — wheeze, stridor, gurgling, snoring?

There is a practical trick that matters. Breathing is partly voluntary, so a patient who knows you are counting will change what they are doing without meaning to. Count while appearing to do something else — keep your fingers on their wrist after you have finished taking the pulse and watch the chest.

And resist the reassurance of a normal number. Sixteen shallow, laboured breaths a minute is not a normal respiratory assessment. It is a patient working hard at a rate that happens to look fine on paper.
read.standard: Respiratory assessment comprises rate and quality. Normal resting adult rate is 12 to 20 breaths per minute; pediatric rates are higher and decline toward adult values with age, with age-band ranges varying between texts. Quality encompasses depth, work of breathing and audible sounds including wheeze, stridor, gurgling and snoring. Because respiration is under partial voluntary control, patient awareness of assessment alters the observed rate; counting is therefore performed unobtrusively, conventionally while maintaining the appearance of pulse assessment. A rate within the normal range does not establish adequate ventilation, as reduced tidal volume and increased work of breathing may coexist with a normal rate.

eli_new.analogy: Ask someone to breathe normally and they immediately cannot. Count them while they think you are still on the wrist.
eli_new.body: The rate is the part that is easy to write in a box, so it gets all the attention. Depth and effort decide whether the patient is actually ventilating, and neither of them has a number.

teach.prompt: Explain how you assess respirations and why you do not tell the patient you are counting.

must_hit.point: Rate and quality together
Normal adult 12 to 20
Counting is done unobtrusively because breathing is partly voluntary
A normal rate with shallow effortful breathing is not normal

teach.model_answer: Rate and quality together. A resting adult is normally 12 to 20; children are faster and infants faster still, falling toward adult values with age. Quality means depth, effort and sound — is the chest really moving, are they using accessory muscles, is there a wheeze or a gurgle. You count without announcing it, usually by keeping your fingers on the wrist after the pulse, because breathing is partly voluntary and a patient who knows you are watching changes what they do. And a normal number is not a normal assessment: sixteen shallow laboured breaths a minute is a patient working hard at a rate that only looks fine on paper.

story.title: Breathe normally
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — 19-year-old male, chest tightness.
story.body:
The student told him he was going to count his breathing, and asked him to breathe normally.

He immediately could not. The next thirty seconds were the least natural breathing anyone in that room had ever done.

The paramedic took the wrist again, said nothing, looked at the chest, and got a completely different number.

concepts.title: Blood pressure by auscultation and palpation
key_points: Systolic is the pressure while the heart contracts; diastolic is the pressure between contractions
Auscultation gives both numbers; palpation gives a systolic only, recorded as systolic over P
Palpation is used where noise or movement makes auscultation impossible
Cuff size matters: a cuff that is too small reads falsely high and one too large reads falsely low
Normal adult systolic is commonly quoted as roughly 90 to 140 mmHg
A useful minimum systolic for a child aged 1 to 10 is 70 plus twice the age in years
Blood pressure is a late sign; it holds until compensation fails
misconceptions: Using an adult cuff on a child or a small adult
Treating a normal blood pressure as evidence that perfusion is fine
Recording a palpated pressure as though both numbers were obtained
exam_favorites: That blood pressure is a late sign

read.plain:
Blood pressure is two numbers. Systolic is the pressure in the arteries while the heart is squeezing; diastolic is what remains between beats.

Auscultation — listening with a stethoscope while letting the cuff down — gives you both. Palpation gives you only a systolic: you feel for the radial pulse returning as the cuff deflates, and you record it as a number over P. You use palpation when the back of a moving ambulance or a noisy scene makes listening impossible, and it is a perfectly legitimate measurement, just an incomplete one.

Cuff size is the error that produces most of the bad readings you will see. Too small a cuff reads falsely high, too large reads falsely low. An adult cuff on a child gives you a number that is confidently wrong, which is worse than no number.

Normal adult systolic is commonly quoted around 90 to 140. For children between one and ten, a widely taught minimum acceptable systolic is 70 plus twice the age in years.

And the most important thing about blood pressure is what it is not. It is a late sign. A young patient will hold a normal pressure while losing a great deal of blood, right up until they cannot, and then it falls quickly. Skin, pulse quality and mental status all move earlier.
read.standard: Blood pressure comprises systolic pressure during ventricular contraction and diastolic pressure between contractions. Auscultation yields both values; palpation yields systolic pressure only, documented as systolic over P, and is indicated where ambient noise or motion precludes auscultation. Cuff selection materially affects accuracy: an undersized cuff produces falsely elevated readings and an oversized cuff falsely reduced readings. Normal adult systolic pressure is commonly cited as approximately 90 to 140 mmHg. A widely taught minimum acceptable systolic pressure for children aged one to ten years is 70 plus twice the age in years. Blood pressure is a late indicator of hypoperfusion, being maintained by compensatory mechanisms until those mechanisms fail, at which point decline may be rapid; cutaneous findings, pulse quality and mental status change earlier.

eli_new.analogy: Blood pressure is the last domino. By the time it falls, the others already have.
eli_new.body: A normal blood pressure feels like permission to relax. It is not. The body defends blood pressure harder than almost anything else, which is exactly why a falling one means the defence has already been overwhelmed.

teach.prompt: Explain the difference between auscultated and palpated blood pressure, and why a normal blood pressure is not reassuring on its own.

must_hit.point: Auscultation gives both numbers, palpation gives systolic only
Cuff too small reads high, too large reads low
Blood pressure is a late sign
Skin, pulse quality and mental status change earlier

teach.model_answer: Auscultation, listening as the cuff deflates, gives you systolic and diastolic. Palpation gives you a systolic only, felt as the radial pulse returns, and is recorded as the number over P — it is legitimate when noise or movement makes listening impossible, just incomplete. Cuff size drives most bad readings: too small reads falsely high, too large falsely low, and an adult cuff on a child gives you a number that is confidently wrong. Normal adult systolic is roughly 90 to 140, and for a child between one and ten a widely taught minimum is 70 plus twice the age in years. And a normal pressure is not reassurance, because it is a late sign — the body defends it until it cannot, so skin, pulse quality and mental status all move first.

story.title: Confidently wrong
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — 6-year-old, fall from a climbing frame.
story.body:
The first pressure came back reassuringly normal and everyone relaxed slightly.

It had been taken with the adult cuff, because it was the one clipped to the monitor.

With the right cuff, the number was considerably lower, and the plan for the call changed.

concepts.title: Pupils
key_points: Assessed for size, equality and reactivity to light
PERRL: Pupils Equal, Round, Reactive to Light
Unequal pupils in a patient with a head injury or altered mental status are a significant finding
Pinpoint pupils are classically associated with opioids
Fixed and dilated pupils are an ominous finding in an unresponsive patient
Some people have naturally unequal pupils, and some have a prosthetic eye or previous surgery — ask if you can
misconceptions: Reporting unequal pupils without checking whether it is normal for that patient
Assessing pupils in bright sunlight and calling them unreactive
Treating pupil findings in isolation from level of consciousness

read.plain:
Pupils are quick, free, and tell you something about the brain and about drugs.

You are checking three things: size, whether the two sides are equal, and whether they react to light. The shorthand is PERRL — pupils equal, round, reactive to light.

Unequal pupils matter most in the company of other findings. In an alert patient with no head injury, a small difference may simply be how they are made. In a patient with a head injury or a falling level of consciousness, inequality is a serious finding and needs to be reported immediately.

Pinpoint pupils are classically opioids, and in an unresponsive patient with slow shallow breathing that picture is fairly characteristic. Fixed and dilated pupils in an unresponsive patient are an ominous sign.

Two practical cautions. Bright sunlight will make pupils small and sluggish and you will report a finding that is really the weather. And some patients have naturally unequal pupils, a prosthetic eye, or previous eye surgery — if there is anyone to ask, ask.
read.standard: Pupillary assessment evaluates size, equality and reactivity to light, summarised as PERRL: pupils equal, round and reactive to light. Anisocoria in the context of head injury or declining level of consciousness constitutes a significant finding warranting immediate communication, whereas minor physiological anisocoria occurs in a proportion of the population. Miosis is classically associated with opioid toxicity, particularly in combination with respiratory depression and reduced responsiveness. Fixed dilated pupils in an unresponsive patient represent an ominous finding. Assessment in bright ambient light produces constricted, apparently sluggish pupils and may generate spurious findings; pre-existing anisocoria, ocular prosthesis and previous ophthalmic surgery should be excluded by history where obtainable.

eli_new.analogy: Two small windows onto the brainstem, and they cost nothing to look at.
eli_new.body: Pupils are most useful alongside something else. On their own they generate false alarms; next to a head injury or a falling level of consciousness, they become one of the more useful things you can report.

teach.prompt: Explain what you assess about pupils and when inequality matters most.

must_hit.point: Size, equality and reactivity to light
Inequality matters most with head injury or altered mental status
Pinpoint suggests opioids
Some people are naturally unequal or have had eye surgery

teach.model_answer: Size, whether the two sides are equal, and whether they react to light — PERRL. Inequality matters most in company: in an alert patient with no head injury a small difference may just be how they are made, but in a head injury or a falling level of consciousness it is a serious finding to report immediately. Pinpoint pupils are classically opioids, especially alongside slow shallow breathing and unresponsiveness, and fixed dilated pupils in an unresponsive patient are ominous. Two cautions: bright sunlight makes pupils small and sluggish and generates false findings, and some patients have naturally unequal pupils, a prosthetic eye or previous surgery, so ask if there is anyone to ask.

story.title: That is how he is
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — 71-year-old male, weakness.
story.body:
One pupil was noticeably larger than the other and the new EMT went slightly pale.

His wife, without looking up, said he had had a cataract operation on that eye in 2011 and it had been like that ever since.

The finding was real. It was also twelve years old, and nobody would have known that without asking.

concepts.title: Skin: colour, temperature and condition
key_points: Colour, temperature and condition — the same three you checked in the primary assessment
Pale, cool and clammy is the classic shock picture, from blood being shunted away from the surface
Cyanosis is a late and serious finding of inadequate oxygenation
Flushed hot dry skin suggests heat illness or fever; flushed can also occur in some poisonings
Mottling, especially in children, is a serious perfusion finding
In patients with darker skin, check the lips, the nail beds, the palms and the conjunctiva
Capillary refill is most useful in children and is affected by cold surroundings
misconceptions: Assessing skin colour only in the face, particularly in darker-skinned patients
Treating cyanosis as an early warning rather than a late one
Using capillary refill as a reliable adult measure in a cold environment
exam_favorites: Where to look in darker skin

read.plain:
Skin is the cheapest and fastest information you will get on any patient, and it costs nothing but the back of your hand.

Three components. Colour, temperature and condition — meaning moisture. Pink, warm and dry is the reassuring combination. Pale, cool and clammy is the classic picture of a patient in shock, because the body pulls blood away from the skin to keep the core supplied, and that decision is made early.

Cyanosis, the blue-grey colour of poor oxygenation, is a late sign. It is serious when you see it, but by the time it appears things have been wrong for a while. Flushed, hot and dry suggests heat illness or fever. Mottling — that blotchy marbled pattern — is a significant perfusion finding, particularly in a child.

One thing worth being deliberate about: assessing colour in patients with darker skin. Looking only at the face will mislead you. Look at the lips, the nail beds, the palms and the conjunctiva, where changes in colour show regardless of pigmentation.

Capillary refill is a useful addition, particularly in children. It is less reliable in adults and it is thrown off by a cold room or a cold night, so do not lean on it alone.
read.standard: Cutaneous assessment comprises colour, temperature and condition. Pallor with cool, diaphoretic skin reflects sympathetically mediated peripheral vasoconstriction and is characteristic of shock, occurring early in compensation. Cyanosis indicates inadequate oxygenation and is a late finding. Flushed, hot, dry skin suggests hyperthermia or febrile illness, and flushing occurs in certain toxidromes. Mottling represents significant perfusion compromise, particularly in pediatric patients. In patients with darker skin pigmentation, colour assessment of the face is unreliable; the lips, nail beds, palms and conjunctivae provide accurate assessment sites. Capillary refill has greatest utility in pediatric assessment, demonstrates reduced reliability in adults, and is confounded by low ambient temperature.

eli_new.analogy: The body turns the outside lights off first. You can see that decision with the back of your hand.
eli_new.body: Because skin findings need no equipment, they get treated as less serious than a number from a machine. They are frequently the earliest thing you will notice, and they are available before you have opened the bag.

teach.prompt: Explain what the skin tells you and how you assess colour in a patient with dark skin.

must_hit.point: Colour, temperature and condition
Pale, cool, clammy is the shock picture
Cyanosis is a late sign
In darker skin check lips, nail beds, palms, conjunctiva

teach.model_answer: Colour, temperature and condition. Pink, warm and dry is what you want; pale, cool and clammy is the classic shock picture, because the body shunts blood from the skin early to protect the core. Cyanosis is a late and serious finding of poor oxygenation. Flushed, hot and dry points to heat illness or fever, and mottling — that blotchy marbled look — is a significant perfusion finding, especially in a child. In patients with darker skin, assessing the face will mislead you: look at the lips, nail beds, palms and conjunctiva, where colour change shows regardless of pigmentation. Capillary refill helps most in children and is unreliable in a cold environment.

story.title: Look at the palms
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — 52-year-old male, feeling faint, shop floor.
story.body:
The student said his colour looked fine, which it did, at his face, under fluorescent light.

The paramedic turned his hand over. The palms were washed out and the nail beds were pale, and his conjunctiva was the colour of paper.

Same patient, same room, completely different assessment — just a different place to look.

concepts.title: Pulse oximetry and capnography as vital signs
key_points: Pulse oximetry estimates the percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen
It tells you about oxygenation and says nothing about ventilation
It is unreliable in poor peripheral perfusion, cold extremities, movement, nail polish and carbon monoxide poisoning
In carbon monoxide poisoning the reading can be falsely reassuring or falsely high
Capnography measures exhaled carbon dioxide and reflects ventilation
Treat the patient, not the number: a good saturation in a patient who looks terrible does not settle the question
misconceptions: Treating a pulse oximetry reading as proof that breathing is adequate
Trusting an oximeter on a cold, poorly perfused finger
Relying on oximetry in a patient pulled from a fire

read.plain:
Two devices that produce numbers, and the useful thing is knowing exactly what each number is about.

Pulse oximetry estimates the percentage of haemoglobin that is carrying oxygen. That is oxygenation. It tells you nothing about whether the patient is moving air — a patient can have an excellent saturation while barely ventilating, right up until they do not.

And it lies in specific, predictable circumstances. A cold finger. Poor peripheral perfusion, which means every shocked patient. Movement. Nail polish. And most dangerously, carbon monoxide poisoning, where the device cannot distinguish what is bound to the haemoglobin and may give you a reassuring number on a patient who is severely poisoned. A patient out of a house fire with a normal saturation has not been cleared by that reading.

Capnography measures the carbon dioxide in exhaled breath, which is a ventilation measurement — it tells you air is actually moving.

The single rule that covers both: treat the patient, not the number. A reassuring reading on a patient who looks terrible means you have a reassuring reading and a patient who looks terrible, and the patient is the more reliable of the two.
read.standard: Pulse oximetry estimates arterial oxyhaemoglobin saturation and therefore reflects oxygenation rather than ventilation; adequate saturation may coexist with grossly inadequate ventilation. Accuracy is degraded by peripheral hypoperfusion, hypothermia of the extremity, motion artefact and nail polish. In carbon monoxide poisoning, conventional pulse oximetry cannot differentiate carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin and may return normal or elevated readings despite severe toxicity. Capnography measures exhaled carbon dioxide and provides direct assessment of ventilation. Both modalities are adjuncts to, and never substitutes for, clinical assessment; discordance between a reassuring numerical value and an unwell patient is resolved in favour of the clinical picture.

eli_new.analogy: The oximeter tells you what is in the tank. It does not tell you whether the engine is turning over.
eli_new.body: Numbers from machines feel more authoritative than what you can see, which is exactly backwards in the situations where the machine is least reliable — cold, shocked, poisoned patients are the ones where the device fails and where you most need to be right.

teach.prompt: Explain what pulse oximetry measures, when it is unreliable, and how capnography differs.

must_hit.point: Oximetry measures oxygenation, not ventilation
Unreliable in poor perfusion, cold, movement, nail polish
Carbon monoxide gives a falsely reassuring reading
Capnography reflects ventilation
Treat the patient, not the number

teach.model_answer: Pulse oximetry estimates the percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen, so it is about oxygenation and says nothing about whether air is moving — a patient can have a fine saturation while barely ventilating. It lies predictably: cold fingers, poor peripheral perfusion, movement, nail polish, and most dangerously carbon monoxide, where it cannot tell what is bound to the haemoglobin and may look normal in a severely poisoned patient. Capnography measures exhaled carbon dioxide, which is a ventilation measurement, so it tells you air is genuinely moving. The rule covering both is treat the patient, not the number: a good reading on a patient who looks terrible just means you have both of those things, and the patient is the more reliable one.

story.title: Ninety-eight percent
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — house fire, one occupant removed by crews.
story.body:
He was confused and had soot around his nose and his saturation read 98 percent.

The student said his oxygen was fine. The officer said it read fine, which is a different sentence.

Carbon monoxide binds to the same haemoglobin, and the probe cannot tell the difference. He went on high-flow oxygen regardless of the number.

concepts.title: Blood glucose measurement
key_points: Indicated in any patient with an altered mental status, and in any known diabetic who is unwell
Hypoglycaemia mimics stroke, intoxication, psychiatric illness and simple confusion
It is one of the few causes of altered mental status an EMT can identify and, within scope, treat
Clean the site, use a fresh lancet, and dispose of sharps immediately and properly
A normal glucose does not explain away an altered patient — it removes one cause
Confirm the exact treatment thresholds and your service's scope for treating them
misconceptions: Omitting a glucose because the patient smells of alcohol
Assuming a normal reading explains the whole presentation
Leaving a used lancet loose on the bag or the stretcher

read.plain:
A blood glucose is one of the highest-value measurements an EMT takes, because it finds a common cause of altered mental status that is otherwise indistinguishable from several serious conditions.

Who gets one: anybody with an altered mental status, and any known diabetic who is unwell for any reason.

The reason it matters so much is what hypoglycaemia looks like. It looks like a stroke — one-sided weakness, slurred speech. It looks like intoxication — aggression, confusion, unsteadiness. It looks like a psychiatric emergency. It looks like a patient who is simply not making sense. Every one of those patients deserves a glucose before anybody settles on an explanation, and the patient who smells of alcohol is the one most likely to be denied one.

The procedure is simple: clean site, fresh lancet, sample, read, and put the sharp straight into the container. Not on the stretcher, not in your pocket.

And read the result carefully. A normal glucose does not explain an altered patient. It removes one cause from the list, which is genuinely useful, and leaves you still looking for the reason.

Treatment thresholds and what you are permitted to give vary by protocol; confirm both.
read.standard: Blood glucose measurement is indicated in all patients with altered mental status and in known diabetic patients presenting with any acute illness. Hypoglycaemia produces presentations clinically indistinguishable from cerebrovascular accident, intoxication, psychiatric emergency and non-specific confusion, and is a correctable cause identifiable at the EMT level. Procedure comprises site cleansing, use of a single-use lancet, sample acquisition and immediate sharps disposal into an approved container. A euglycaemic result excludes hypoglycaemia as a cause but does not account for altered mental status of other aetiology, and assessment continues. Treatment thresholds and permitted interventions are protocol-determined.

eli_new.analogy: It is a stroke, a psychiatric emergency, or a drunk patient — until a drop of blood says it was none of those.
eli_new.body: The patient least likely to get a glucose is the patient who smells of alcohol, and that is precisely the patient in whom missing hypoglycaemia is most likely and most harmful.

teach.prompt: Explain who gets a blood glucose and why hypoglycaemia is so easy to miss.

must_hit.point: Any altered mental status, and any unwell diabetic
It mimics stroke, intoxication and psychiatric illness
A normal result removes one cause but does not explain the patient
Dispose of the sharp immediately

teach.model_answer: Any patient with an altered mental status, and any known diabetic who is unwell. It matters because hypoglycaemia looks like other things — one-sided weakness and slurred speech like a stroke, confusion and aggression like intoxication, or a psychiatric emergency — and it is one of very few causes an EMT can both find and, within scope, treat. The patient who smells of alcohol is the one most often denied a glucose and the one in whom missing it does most harm. Clean site, fresh lancet, sharp straight into the container. And a normal reading removes one cause rather than explaining the patient, so you keep looking.

story.title: He smelled of drink
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — male, intoxicated, found in a doorway.
story.body:
He smelled strongly of alcohol, he was aggressive, and he was not making sense. Everybody had already decided what this was.

Your partner did a glucose anyway, mostly out of habit.

It was low. He had been drinking, and he was also hypoglycaemic, and the second of those was the one that was going to kill him.

concepts.title: Temperature
key_points: Taken where the history suggests it matters: fever, heat illness, cold exposure, infection, and in the very young and very old
A hot patient is not always febrile: consider environmental heat illness as well as infection
A cold patient may be hypothermic even in mild weather if they have been down for a long time or are elderly, thin or intoxicated
In hypothermia, handle the patient gently and take a longer look for a pulse
The route of measurement affects the reading; record which route you used
misconceptions: Assuming a hot patient has an infection
Ruling out hypothermia because the weather is mild
Handling a hypothermic patient roughly

read.plain:
Temperature is not measured on everyone, and the skill is knowing when it earns its place: a patient who feels hot or cold, a suspected infection, heat exposure, cold exposure, and both ends of the age range, where temperature regulation is least reliable.

A hot patient is not automatically an infected patient. Heat illness produces a hot patient too, and the distinction matters enormously because the treatments diverge. Look at the context — what were they doing, where, and for how long.

A cold patient is the one people miss. Hypothermia does not require snow. An elderly person who has been on a kitchen floor overnight in a house with the heating off can be profoundly hypothermic in autumn. So can someone thin, or intoxicated, or simply down for a long time.

If you do have a hypothermic patient, two things change. Handle them gently, because a very cold heart is irritable. And look longer for a pulse than you normally would, because it may be very slow and very weak.

Finally, record the route. An oral, tympanic and skin temperature are not the same measurement, and the number is only interpretable if the receiving clinician knows how it was taken.
read.standard: Temperature measurement is indicated where history or examination suggests thermal dysregulation: suspected infection, hyperthermic or hypothermic exposure, and at the extremes of age where thermoregulation is impaired. Hyperthermia may reflect environmental heat illness rather than febrile infection, and the distinction alters management substantially. Hypothermia occurs in the absence of extreme ambient cold, particularly in elderly, cachectic or intoxicated patients and following prolonged immobility; mild ambient temperature does not exclude it. In the hypothermic patient, gentle handling is required owing to myocardial irritability, and pulse assessment is prolonged as bradycardia and reduced pulse volume may render a pulse difficult to detect. The measurement route materially affects the value obtained and should be documented alongside the reading.

eli_new.analogy: Hypothermia does not need snow. It needs time, and a floor.
eli_new.body: The mental model of hypothermia is mountains and blizzards, which is why the elderly patient found on a kitchen floor in October gets missed. Time on a cold surface does most of the work.

teach.prompt: Explain when you would take a temperature and why a cold patient can be missed in mild weather.

must_hit.point: Fever, heat or cold exposure, infection, very young and very old
A hot patient may be heat illness rather than infection
Hypothermia occurs in mild weather after long exposure
Handle gently and check the pulse longer

teach.model_answer: You take one where the history makes it matter: suspected fever or infection, heat exposure, cold exposure, and at both ends of the age range where temperature regulation is poorest. A hot patient is not automatically infected — heat illness produces a hot patient too and the treatments diverge, so read the context. And a cold patient is the one that gets missed: hypothermia does not need snow, just time on a cold surface, so an elderly person down overnight in an unheated house can be profoundly hypothermic in autumn. If they are hypothermic, handle them gently because a cold heart is irritable, and look longer than usual for a pulse. Record which route you used, because oral, tympanic and skin readings are not interchangeable.

story.title: October, indoors
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — 83-year-old female, fallen, unable to get up, found by a neighbour.
story.body:
It was October and it was not cold outside. The heating had been off for two days because she could not reach the switch after she fell.

She had been on the kitchen tiles for somewhere around fourteen hours.

Her temperature was the finding that reorganised the whole call, and nobody had expected it in that weather.
